papers.title: Needwise: Generation-Free Conversational Recommendation from Need-Level Typed Decisions
papers.authors: Sungchul Kim, Weixiao Huang, Mekala Raja Sekhar Reddy, Amrutha Srinivasan
papers.abstract: Conversational recommenders must rank items against needs that catalogs record only in part, while users add, withdraw and reverse needs and switch between requests. LLM rankers re-read the dialogue at every turn: they are slow, and their ordering does not show which needs an item meets. We show that a conversational recommender can be built from typed decisions instead: named questions over fixed options, answered with option probabilities rather than generated text. On each turn, one typed request maps the message onto the catalog's fields, keeps what no field expresses in the user's words, and decides how the turn changes each earlier need. Needwise then ranks candidates must-first: the needs on the kind of item, its place and its price form a tier, and within it one holistic decision and need-level verdicts (supported, contradicted or unknown) are combined with equal weight (Needwise-HF). With the graded attributes withheld from the records, so that needs must be inferred from names, descriptions and reviews, Needwise-HF ranks Google Local requests significantly better than GPT-6 Sol (0.383 against 0.343 nDCG@10) and is not significantly different from the strongest LLM ranker on Google Local and Yelp; these comparisons keep their sign under every treatment of unrecorded attributes we test. It costs a fraction of GPT-6 Sol's API price and answers in 2.5 s at the median on Google Local, against 5.6 s for GPT-6 Sol. In conversations, the typed state keeps the ranking across switches and returns, but it recognizes only 19-27% of withdrawn needs.
papers.summary: In conversational recommendation, users add, drop, withdraw, and reverse needs, while catalogs record only some of the attributes. Typical LLM rankers reread the whole dialogue at every turn, which is slow and does not show which needs an item actually meets. The new system maps each turn onto typed decisions over fixed options, then ranks must-first by item type, place, and price. On Google Local, Needwise-HF reaches 0.383 nDCG@10, ahead of GPT-6 Sol at 0.343. Its median response is 2.5 seconds, compared with 5.6 seconds for the latter. The typed state keeps the ranking across topic switches, but it still recognizes only a limited share of withdrawn needs.

papers.title: SARA: An Auditor-in-the-Loop LLM Recommender for Sustainability Reports
papers.authors: Lars Hillebrand, Thiago B. F. de Oliveira, Tim Dilmaghani, Mohamed Khaled, Writwick Das, Rafet Sifa
papers.abstract: Auditing corporate sustainability reports requires assurance professionals to map a company-specific checklist drawn from roughly 1,700 regulatory requirements onto the relevant passages of lengthy, repeatedly revised draft reports and to judge compliance. We present SARA (Sustainability Reporting Assistant), a human-in-the-loop recommender system delivered as a Microsoft Word add-in that recommends, for each requirement, the passages addressing it and predicts a compliance verdict while keeping the auditor in full control. SARA casts auditing as content-based recommendation over a fixed regulatory taxonomy and makes per-requirement large language model (LLM) matching cheaper, faster, and more accurate through topic-prediction filtering: on expert-annotated reports, it reduces matching cost about sixfold and runtime by 42% versus feeding the full report to the LLM. It is in production use across PwC Germany's sustainability-assurance practice.
papers.summary: Auditing sustainability reports means mapping a checklist drawn from about 1,700 regulatory requirements onto long, repeatedly revised drafts, then judging compliance. The new system is a Word add-in that, for each requirement, recommends the relevant passages and predicts a compliance verdict, while the auditor stays in control. It first predicts a topic and sends only passages from that sub-topic to the language model. On two expert-annotated reports, that is about six times cheaper than feeding the full report to the model, cuts runtime by 42%, and raises precision and F1 by 4.4 and 3.1 points. It is already in production in PwC Germany's sustainability-assurance practice.

papers.title: MADRec: Reliable Multi-Agent Reasoning with Evidence-Grounded Debate for Recommendation
papers.authors: Zunlong Liu, Weijie Feng, Jingzhi Li, Lei Zhu, Zhiyong Cheng, Meng Wang
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming recommender systems from conventional preference matching toward reasoning-driven and explainable decision-making. Multi-agent collaboration further advances this paradigm by distributing recommendation reasoning across specialized agents. However, existing frameworks rarely assess the reliability of intermediate reasoning during collaboration, allowing erroneous judgments to propagate across agents and ultimately degrade recommendation quality. To address this issue, we propose Multi-Agent Debate-based Recommendation (MADRec), an evidence-grounded multi-agent framework that enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning. MADRec consists of three coordinated modules. First, the Multi-Agent Debate (MAD) module enables an Interaction Agent and a Semantic Agent to analyze interaction signals and content-level semantic signals from complementary perspectives, generating diverse recommendation judgments through structured debate. Second, the Evidence-Grounded Retrieval-Augmented Reasoning (EG-RAR) module grounds the Semantic Agent's reasoning in item-level evidence and refines candidate scores by assessing how well the evidence supports the corresponding semantic claims. Third, the Judge-based Ranking Calibration (JRC) module leverages debate-derived reliability cues to adaptively calibrate interaction-based and semantic ranking results for the final recommendation. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that MADRec consistently outperforms competitive baselines and enhances the reliability of multi-agent recommendation reasoning.
papers.summary: In multi-agent recommendation, if intermediate reasoning is not checked, a wrong judgment can pass from one agent to another and distort the final ranking. The new framework has an interaction agent and a semantic agent debate in a structured way, grounds semantic claims in item-level evidence, and then calibrates the ranking with reliability cues from the debate. On MovieLens 1M, Amazon-Book, and Amazon-Beauty, Recall@10 rises 14.15%, 32.79%, and 22.77% over the strongest non-MADRec baseline. When the two branches disagree, the judge also tends to put more weight on the better-performing one.

papers.title: GuardAgent: A Memory-Augmented Agentic Framework for Adaptive Detection of Adversarial Promotions in LLM-Based Recommendation
papers.authors: Shiyi Yang, Xinshu Li, Chen Wang, Xiwei Xu, Liming Zhu, Lina Yao
papers.abstract: In traditional recommender systems (RSs), textual information typically serves as auxiliary signals for representation learning. In contrast, in LLM-based RSs, textual information becomes the primary medium for recommendation generation through semantic understanding and reasoning. This shift fundamentally changes the attack surface, making promotion-driven manipulations more feasible, effective, and harder to detect. However, effectively detecting such attacks remains largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we present the first systematic study on detecting promotion-driven attacks against LLM-based RSs, aiming to safeguard next-generation recommendation platforms. Specifically, we propose GuardAgent, a novel LLM-powered agentic detection framework that operates through a loop of Perception, Action, Reflection and Memory. In contrast to conventional LLM-based detectors that function in a static, one-off, and opaque fashion, GuardAgent continually learns and self-evolves to adapt to unseen threat patterns while generating explainable reasoning traces and outcomes. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that GuardAgent achieves state-of-the-art generalization performance, laying the foundation for robust and trustworthy recommendation in practical settings.
papers.summary: Promotion attacks on LLM recommenders often rewrite titles or descriptions that are visible at inference time, so detectors built for training-time poisoning offer little help. The new detector runs a loop of perception, action, reflection, and memory: it revises decision rules from paired false alarms and missed detections, and leaves an auditable reasoning trace. On Amazon product and Yelp business data, its detection F1 reaches 0.92 and 0.81, ahead of retrieval-based in-context learning and other controls. On previously unseen agentic attacks, the average detection rate is 100%, with negligible false positives.

scenario: Today's generative-recommendation papers split between generating less and putting generation to work in auditing, debate, and defense. Some fold conversational needs into typed decisions over fixed options, so an LLM does not have to rerank from scratch at every turn. Some recommend passages for each regulatory requirement inside a sustainability report, right in Word. Others let two agents debate and then check claims against evidence, so an intermediate mistake is less likely to reach the final list. Against attacks that rewrite titles or descriptions to buy exposure, a detector keeps revising its rules through reflection so it can follow new tactics.
